title: Wait Time
author: Jonathan Nicolas Jarrett-Kerr
summary: Jarrett-Kerr revisits and extends an earlier piece on 'name-end questioning' (his term for cold calling), prompted by a reader suggestion from Tom Sherrington that the pause should be built into the naming convention itself ('Question, Pause, Name'). He clarifies that wait time -- which he also calls 'think time' when speaking to students -- is not always necessary; it matters for genuine checks of understanding but not for low-stakes retrieval like reporting what a partner said in a paired discussion. He is candid that wait time does not come naturally to him, since he values pace and has spent years eliminating dead time in his lessons, and describes a simple metacognitive fix: silently reminding himself after every question that wait time matters, which alone was enough to leave the right amount of space. He extends the concept beyond verbal questioning to mini-whiteboards and diagnostic quizzes, describing a consistent 'question, wait time, trigger' pattern, and credits Adam Boxer with a practical calibration heuristic: if a named student is still visibly thinking, the wait was too short; if they answer instantly, too much wait was given. He closes by framing wait time, combined with name-end questioning, as one of the most inclusive things a teacher can do in a classroom, because it signals to every student that their thinking is valued, not just the thinking of the fastest hands.
points: Jarrett-Kerr corrects an implicit overgeneralization in his own earlier framework: wait time is not universally required for every question type -- it matters for genuine checks of understanding, but not for low-stakes retrieval tasks like reporting a partner's answer.

His practical fix for a personal weakness (valuing lesson pace over think time) is a simple metacognitive cue -- silently telling himself after each question that wait time matters -- which he reports was sufficient on its own to correct the habit.

He generalizes wait time beyond verbal questioning into a repeatable 'question, wait time, trigger' pattern used with mini-whiteboards and diagnostic quizzes, positioning it as a general instructional rhythm rather than a questioning-specific technique.

He credits Adam Boxer with a concrete calibration heuristic for wait-time length: if the named student is still visibly thinking when called on, the wait was too short; if they answer instantly, too much wait was given.
quotes: Tom noted that, if the goal is to be totally unambiguous through nomenclature, the pause and the crucial thinking time would be in the name itself, and suggested “Question, Pause, Name” as an alternative.

Wait time is not an easy strategy. I know this from personal experience. I like pace in my lessons, and I worked hard over the years at removing dead time... I think a by-product of that is that wait time got forgotten.

Even so, wait time combined with name-end questioning is, in my opinion, one of the most inclusive things a teacher can use in the classroom. It is telling students: your thoughts matter. All of your thoughts matter. I value your thinking.
I use the same pattern with colour signalling during my end-of-lesson diagnostic quizzes. Question, wait time, trigger, students answer.

A useful tip I picked up from Adam Boxer on the length of wait time: if you say the name and the student is still thinking, the wait time was too short. If they immediately knew the answer, too much wait was given.
For me, having an internal mantra helps. Reminding myself post-question that wait time matters is enough to leave the right amount of space.
